bibl.title: An overview of the uses of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS)

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: where per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances are used, what job they do there, and how much of what is knowable at all from the registers that record chemical use
span.quote: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are of concern because of their very high persistence and impacts on human and environmental health. Currently, many different PFAS (on the order of several thousands) are used in a wide range of applications and there is no comprehensive source of information on the many individual substances and their functions in different applications. Here we provide a broad overview of many use categories where PFAS have been employed and for which function; we also specify which PFAS have been used and discuss the magnitude of the uses. Our compilation is not exhaustive, but it was still possible to demonstrate that PFAS are used in almost all industry branches and many consumer products. In total, more than 200 use categories and subcategories were identified for more than 1400 individual PFAS.

span.label: in which use categories PFAS have been employed and for which function, which individual substances, and whether the uses can be ranked by quantity
span.quote: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are of concern because of their very high persistence and impacts on human and environmental health. Currently, many different PFAS (on the order of several thousands) are used in a wide range of applications and there is no comprehensive source of information on the many individual substances and their functions in different applications. Here we provide a broad overview of many use categories where PFAS have been employed and for which function; we also specify which PFAS have been used and discuss the magnitude of the uses. Our compilation is not exhaustive, but it was still possible to demonstrate that PFAS are used in almost all industry branches and many consumer products. In total, more than 200 use categories and subcategories were identified for more than 1400 individual PFAS.

span.label: more than 200 use categories and subcategories for more than 1400 individual PFAS - five times the previous standard compilation - with the function and the enabling property named for each, and every source's blind spot stated and where possible sized
span.quote: In the present study, more than 200 uses in 64 use categories were identified for more than 1400 individual PFAS. This means that the present study encompasses five times as many uses (counted as use categories plus subcategories) than included by Kissa (2001). This shows that the present study goes much further than simply updating this previous work.

span.label: existence
span.quote: In the present study, more than 200 uses in 64 use categories were identified for more than 1400 individual PFAS. This means that the present study encompasses five times as many uses (counted as use categories plus subcategories) than included by Kissa (2001). This shows that the present study goes much further than simply updating this previous work.

span.label: a class of thousands of extremely persistent substances used across almost every industry branch, whose extent cannot be established because the quantities are commercial secrets and the registers exempt whole categories
span.quote: Under the TSCA, the Chemical Data Reporting lists under “volume” the amount of a substance in a certain sector and function category or product category. However, more than 80% of the volume entries in the Chemical Data Reporting database are CBI. The certainty of the available information is therefore low, but a general statement is still possible.

span.label: a compilation from risk profiles, monographs, the US TSCA Chemical Data Reporting, the Nordic SPIN product registers, patent literature via SciFindern, manufacturer factsheets and analytical product studies - each source labelled in the tables by what kind of evidence it is
span.term: a compilation from risk profiles, monographs, the US TSCA Chemical Data Reporting, the Nordic SPIN product registers, patent literature via SciFindern, manufacturer factsheets and analytical product studies - each source labelled in the tables by what kind of evidence it is
span.quote: Through the patents it was possible to determine in which applications PFAS may be used. While it is not possible to determine whether licenses for a patent have been obtained, the status of the patent (e.g. active, withdrawn, expired, not yet granted) can be determined. Active patents become expensive for their owners over the years. Representatives from CAS informed us that it is very likely that a patent is still in use if it is still paid for after 10 to 15 years. After 20 years, a patent expires, which means that the invention can be used by others free of cost. Note that many patents cover not just a specific substance, but rather a basic structure to which different functional groups can be attached. The SciFindern experts give CAS numbers to those substances whose existence has been proven by the registrants. Such a proof can be a physical method or the description in a patent document example or claim. Still, it is not always clear which substances are actually used in practice.

span.label: PFAS are 100 to 1000 times more expensive than hydrocarbon alternatives, so they are bought only where extreme stability, wide temperature range or very low surface energy are required. The carbon-fluorine bond supplies all three - and the same bond is why the substance does not degrade after the product is discarded. Utility and persistence are not correlated here, they are the same fact
span.term: the property that sells it is the property that keeps it
span.quote: PFAS are costly to produce (e.g. fluorosurfactants are 100–1000 times more expensive than conventional hydrocarbon surfactants per unit volume) and therefore are often used where other substances cannot deliver the required performance, or where PFAS can be used in a much smaller amount and with the same performance as a higher amount of a non-fluorinated chemical. Examples are uses that operate over wide temperature ranges or uses that require extremely stable and non-reactive substances. The C-F bonds in PFAS lead to very stable substances, a feature that also makes them very persistent in the environment.

span.label: every quantity in this paper comes from a register with a declared exclusion: a reporting threshold of 11.34 t at a single site, statutory exemptions for foodstuffs medicines and cosmetics, no duty to declare solid articles, and confidentiality over more than 80% of the volumes. The inventory is therefore a map of the disclosure regime, and the paper says so instead of presenting it as a map of use
span.term: an inventory bounded by what registers agree to record
span.quote: The data from the US are only partly helpful, because a large part of the reported amounts is CBI and only substances above 11.34 t at a single site have been reported. Although in some use categories large quantities of PFAS are employed, it is difficult to compare the amounts, because the unreported amounts due to CBI could be much larger than the non-confidential reported amounts. The extent of the uncertainties in the SPIN database due to the CBI cannot be estimated with the available data, but could be large.

span.label: PFAS membership has been defined three times, each wider or narrower in a different place, and every number in this literature - how many substances, how many uses, how much tonnage - is a number under one of them. The paper states which one it uses and exactly where it departs from the others
span.term: a class boundary that moves the count
span.quote: In contrast to the definition by Buck et al. (2011), the present study also includes i) substances where a perfluorocarbon chain is connected with functional groups on both ends, ii) aromatic substances that have perfluoroalkyl moieties on the side chains, and iii) fluorinated cycloaliphatic substances. More specifically, the present study focuses on polymeric PFAS with the -CF2- moiety and non-polymeric PFAS with the -CF2-CF2- moiety. It does not include non-polymeric substances that only contain a -CF3 or -CF2- moiety, with the exception of perfluoroalkylethers and per- and polyfluoroalkylether-based substances.

span.label: two voluntary programmes removed the best-known PFAS from two manufacturers' portfolios; other companies were not prevented from taking the market, enforcement was very limited, and substances that break down into the same acids remain in medical devices, apparel and semiconductor manufacture
span.quote: However, other companies have not been prevented from taking over the market, and there has been very limited enforcement of the actual phase-out through regulation. A recent article revealed that PFAS that can break down into PFOA and PFOS are still in use in the US. Those uses include coatings for medical devices, apparel, and other industries, and equipment in pharmaceutical companies. PFAS that can break down into PFOA and PFOS are also still used in semiconductor and electronics companies.

span.label: the searches were not exhaustive in any source, and the authors say there are many more reports, studies, patents, safety data sheets and databases than those used
span.quote: The searches were not exhaustive in any of the sources described, and there are still many more reports, scientific studies, patents, safety data sheets and databases with information on the uses of PFAS than the ones cited here or in the ESI-1.

span.label: more than 80% of the volume entries in the US Chemical Data Reporting database are confidential, so the certainty of the quantity information is low
span.quote: Under the TSCA, the Chemical Data Reporting lists under “volume” the amount of a substance in a certain sector and function category or product category. However, more than 80% of the volume entries in the Chemical Data Reporting database are CBI. The certainty of the available information is therefore low, but a general statement is still possible.

span.label: the extent of the uncertainty introduced by confidentiality in the SPIN database cannot be estimated from the available data and could be large
span.quote: The data from the US are only partly helpful, because a large part of the reported amounts is CBI and only substances above 11.34 t at a single site have been reported. Although in some use categories large quantities of PFAS are employed, it is difficult to compare the amounts, because the unreported amounts due to CBI could be much larger than the non-confidential reported amounts. The extent of the uncertainties in the SPIN database due to the CBI cannot be estimated with the available data, but could be large.

span.label: the Nordic data may not represent other regions - the registers exempt foodstuffs, medicines and cosmetics, and there is no PFAS or fluoropolymer production there
span.quote: It should be noted that the data from these Nordic countries may not be representative of other parts of the world. One reason is that only non-confidential data are included, that substances in foodstuffs, medicinal products, and cosmetics do not have to be declared (see Section 2.2.2) and that there is no fluoropolymer or PFAS production in these countries.

span.label: neither database covers PFAS in finished articles, which removes most of the manufacturing done outside the EU and US
span.quote: PFAS used in articles, which are manufactured mainly in Asia or other countries outside the EU or the US, may also not appear in large amounts in the SPIN or Chemical Data Reporting database, simply because the databases do not contain information on PFAS in articles.

span.label: seventy PFAS from the Chinese inventory are absent from this one because no information on their intended use was provided
span.quote: A recent publication lists e.g. seventy PFAS from the Inventory of Existing Chemical Substances Produced or Imported in China (IECSC) that are not in the North American and European chemical inventories. These PFAS are also not in our inventory, because no information on their intended use was provided.

span.label: some register categories were too broad to map onto the study's use categories, and those substances and their quantities were dropped
span.quote: Still, there were some use categories (especially from the Chemical Data Reporting database under the TSCA) that were so broad that we were not able to assign them to any category in our list. Examples are “surface active agents in all other basic inorganic chemical manufacturing”, or “functional fluids in wholesale and retail trade”. The PFAS listed under such categories and their quantities were not, therefore, considered in the present study.

span.label: in 4% of cases the function of the PFAS could not be determined and in 21% the property needed to fulfil that function could not be determined
span.quote: However, as can be seen from the question marks in the Appendix it was not always possible to determine why PFAS were used or needed in a particular case. In 4% of the cases we could not clarify which function the PFAS fulfil in the use category or subcategory, and in 21% of the cases we could not clarify which property is needed to fulfil the mentioned function. For example, we do not know exactly why PFAS are employed in the ventilation of respiratory airways, in brake-pad additives, and in resilient linoleum.

span.label: uses may be missing entirely - PFAS were found in climbing ropes and no information was found on climbing harnesses, and no industry interviews were possible
span.quote: Another area of uncertainty originates from unidentified uses. We found, for example, that PFAS are used in climbing ropes. It therefore cannot be excluded that they are also used in climbing harnesses, but no information was found on this. We did not have the capacity to conduct interviews with industry representatives who might have revealed additional information. We were similarly limited when it came to evaluating the copious amount of information about PFAS uses, for example in reports, scientific papers and patents. Therefore, not all PFAS uses might have been identified in the present study.

span.label: the coverage claim for the general use categories is qualitative, and subcategories are quite possibly missing
span.quote: Overall, we assume that there are no major gaps in the general use categories. However, it is quite possible that subcategories are missing. Among the uses of which we are aware, there may also be some uses where PFAS are no longer employed.

span.label: industrial blends can be 80% of the registered substance, so impurities, reaction by-products and degradation products are present alongside the intended PFAS
span.quote: The substances listed in ESI-1 under U or U* are also those that were intentionally used in the products. However, impurities, reaction products upon mixing the ingredients, and degradation products of the intentionally added PFAS might also be present in products. Industrial blends are rarely pure, but can be only 80% of the registered substance, so 20% can be impurities, reaction by-products, degradation products etc.

span.label: REACH data covering more countries were excluded because its tonnage bands attach to substances rather than to use categories - the wrong unit for this question
span.quote: Data from REACH that would have covered more countries than the data from the SPIN database are not shown, because the tonnage bands in REACH refer to the substances and not to use categories. Accordingly, only in those cases where a substance has only one use would it have been possible to obtain useful information for this study, which would have created a lot of uncertainty in the data.

span.label: the essential-use test, carried from the Montreal Protocol's ozone regime into chemicals policy, where the question becomes which uses of a persistent substance justify themselves rather than whether the substance is harmful
span.quote: However, there are specific uses that make an immediate ban of all PFAS impractical. Some specific uses of PFAS may currently be essential to health, safety or the functioning of today’s society for which alternatives so far do not exist. On the other hand, if some uses of PFAS are found to be non-essential, they could be eliminated without having to first find alternatives that provide an adequate function and performance. To determine which uses of PFAS are essential and which are not, the concept of “essential use,” as defined under the Montreal Protocol, has recently been further developed for PFAS, including illustrative case studies for several major use categories of PFAS.

span.label: suspect-screening by accurate mass spectrometry, supplied here with a list of exact monoisotopic masses per use category so that a laboratory can look for substances nobody has yet measured
span.quote: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are of concern because of their very high persistence and impacts on human and environmental health. Currently, many different PFAS (on the order of several thousands) are used in a wide range of applications and there is no comprehensive source of information on the many individual substances and their functions in different applications. Here we provide a broad overview of many use categories where PFAS have been employed and for which function; we also specify which PFAS have been used and discuss the magnitude of the uses. Our compilation is not exhaustive, but it was still possible to demonstrate that PFAS are used in almost all industry branches and many consumer products. In total, more than 200 use categories and subcategories were identified for more than 1400 individual PFAS.

span.label: commercial market reports excluded from the study entirely, although they cover the quantities the study most wants
span.note: eliminates: an unverifiable figure entering the inventory - the reports do not state their sources, so a number taken from one could not be checked by anyone, including the authors · outcome: held
span.quote: A variety of non-verified commercial market reports exist for PFAS. Examples are the Fluorotelomer Market Report, Fluorochemicals Market Report or the Perfluoropolyether Market Report from Global Market Insights. The information from these reports is not included in this study as these reports do not state their information sources and thus cannot be verified.

span.label: REACH data excluded, despite covering more countries than the Nordic registers used, because its tonnage bands attach to substances and not to use categories
span.note: eliminates: a quantity reported against the wrong denominator being read as a use-category quantity - only single-use substances would have been informative and the rest would have carried invented precision · outcome: held
span.quote: Data from REACH that would have covered more countries than the data from the SPIN database are not shown, because the tonnage bands in REACH refer to the substances and not to use categories. Accordingly, only in those cases where a substance has only one use would it have been possible to obtain useful information for this study, which would have created a lot of uncertainty in the data.

span.label: every substance-use link labelled by the KIND of evidence behind it - P for patent, D for analytically detected, U for a reported use - and the three shares reported
span.note: eliminates: a patented possibility and an observed use counting as the same fact; 42% of the 2400 links are patents and the reader is told which · outcome: held
span.quote: Of the 2400 links between individual PFAS and assigned uses, around 42% of the links were obtained from patents, 27% from studies that detected PFAS in products and 31% from publications that reported actual uses.

span.label: the study's own use categories compared against the independently built SPIN category list, to test whether whole categories had been missed
span.note: eliminates: the compilation's coverage resting on the compilers' own imagination - an external classification is asked what it has that this one does not, and it had three · outcome: partial
span.quote: An important question is whether the majority of the use categories is covered in the present study or whether important use categories are still missing. It is difficult to answer such a question quantitatively, but a qualitative indication is possible when the use categories of the SPIN database are compared to the categories that were already identified. Both categories match very well; only three categories had to be added to accommodate data from the SPIN database in the ESI-1 appropriately.

span.label: the count of substances stated as a count of what this search found, next to the figure a reader would otherwise take it for
span.note: eliminates: the study's own reach being read as the size of the market - said before the numbers rather than after them · outcome: held
span.quote: It should be noted that the number of PFAS reflects the number that we have identified in the present study, and not the number of substances on the market or available for a certain use. For half of the use categories, we have identified more than 20 PFAS, and for seven use categories more than 100 PFAS.

span.label: two use categories reported with NO substances identified rather than dropped - ammunition and the nuclear industry
span.note: eliminates: a category disappearing because the search failed in it; the empty result is printed where a reader can see which categories it applies to · outcome: held
span.quote: There are also two categories where no specific substances were identified. These are “ammunition” and “nuclear industry”.

span.label: the 11.34 t single-site reporting threshold under TSCA, below which no substance appears in the volume data at all
span.note: eliminates: substances below the 11.34 t single-site threshold - they do not appear in the volume data at all, so the totals are a floor and not an estimate · outcome: absent-declared-unreported
span.quote: Manufacturers and importers that produced chemicals in amounts exceeding 25’000 pounds (11.34 metric tons, t) at a site in the US between 2012 and 2015 were obliged to report to the US Environmental Protection Agency (US EPA) in 2016 (data for 2016 to 2019 will be reported in 2020). The data reported in 2016 (available in CSV files) included for each reported substance the name, Chemical Abstracts Service (CAS) registry number and product categories for consumer and commercial uses and sectors, as well as function categories for industrial processing and use. The masses (tonnages) used and exported also had to be reported; however, they are in most cases confidential business information (CBI).

span.label: the statutory exemptions in the Nordic registers - foodstuffs, medicinal products, cosmetics, solid articles, and anything under 0.1 t per year
span.note: eliminates: products under the statutory exemptions - foodstuffs, medicinal products, cosmetics, solid articles and anything under 0.1 t a year are absent from the Nordic registers by law · outcome: absent-declared-unreported
span.quote: There are several cases in which substances do not need to be registered. For example, Denmark, Finland, Norway and Sweden exempt products that come under legislation on foodstuffs and medicinal products from mandatory declaration. Furthermore, the duty to declare products to the product registers does not apply to cosmetic products. In addition, there is in principle no requirement to declare solid processed articles to any of the registers. There is also a general exemption from the duty to declare chemicals in Sweden, Finland and Norway, if the quantity produced or imported is less than 0.1 t per year (in Finland no exact amount is given).

span.label: PFAS
span.quote: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are of concern because of their very high persistence and impacts on human and environmental health. Currently, many different PFAS (on the order of several thousands) are used in a wide range of applications and there is no comprehensive source of information on the many individual substances and their functions in different applications. Here we provide a broad overview of many use categories where PFAS have been employed and for which function; we also specify which PFAS have been used and discuss the magnitude of the uses. Our compilation is not exhaustive, but it was still possible to demonstrate that PFAS are used in almost all industry branches and many consumer products. In total, more than 200 use categories and subcategories were identified for more than 1400 individual PFAS.

span.label: persistent
span.quote: PFAS are costly to produce (e.g. fluorosurfactants are 100–1000 times more expensive than conventional hydrocarbon surfactants per unit volume) and therefore are often used where other substances cannot deliver the required performance, or where PFAS can be used in a much smaller amount and with the same performance as a higher amount of a non-fluorinated chemical. Examples are uses that operate over wide temperature ranges or uses that require extremely stable and non-reactive substances. The C-F bonds in PFAS lead to very stable substances, a feature that also makes them very persistent in the environment.

span.label: CBI
span.quote: Under the TSCA, the Chemical Data Reporting lists under “volume” the amount of a substance in a certain sector and function category or product category. However, more than 80% of the volume entries in the Chemical Data Reporting database are CBI. The certainty of the available information is therefore low, but a general statement is still possible.

span.label: SPIN database
span.quote: The data from the US are only partly helpful, because a large part of the reported amounts is CBI and only substances above 11.34 t at a single site have been reported. Although in some use categories large quantities of PFAS are employed, it is difficult to compare the amounts, because the unreported amounts due to CBI could be much larger than the non-confidential reported amounts. The extent of the uncertainties in the SPIN database due to the CBI cannot be estimated with the available data, but could be large.

span.label: patents
span.quote: Through the patents it was possible to determine in which applications PFAS may be used. While it is not possible to determine whether licenses for a patent have been obtained, the status of the patent (e.g. active, withdrawn, expired, not yet granted) can be determined. Active patents become expensive for their owners over the years. Representatives from CAS informed us that it is very likely that a patent is still in use if it is still paid for after 10 to 15 years. After 20 years, a patent expires, which means that the invention can be used by others free of cost. Note that many patents cover not just a specific substance, but rather a basic structure to which different functional groups can be attached. The SciFindern experts give CAS numbers to those substances whose existence has been proven by the registrants. Such a proof can be a physical method or the description in a patent document example or claim. Still, it is not always clear which substances are actually used in practice.

span.label: use categories
span.quote: Still, there were some use categories (especially from the Chemical Data Reporting database under the TSCA) that were so broad that we were not able to assign them to any category in our list. Examples are “surface active agents in all other basic inorganic chemical manufacturing”, or “functional fluids in wholesale and retail trade”. The PFAS listed under such categories and their quantities were not, therefore, considered in the present study.

span.label: articles
span.quote: PFAS used in articles, which are manufactured mainly in Asia or other countries outside the EU or the US, may also not appear in large amounts in the SPIN or Chemical Data Reporting database, simply because the databases do not contain information on PFAS in articles.

span.label: essential uses
span.quote: The approach of allowing PFAS only in “essential uses”, as suggested for example in the EU strategy paper “Elements for an EU-strategy for PFAS”, will not be easy to implement if regulators try to assess all uses individually. An alternative approach could be to deem all PFAS uses as “non-essential” unless producers or users make a convincing case for essentiality, and that authorities set a sunset clause on “essential uses”.

span.label: fluorosurfactants
span.quote: PFAS are costly to produce (e.g. fluorosurfactants are 100–1000 times more expensive than conventional hydrocarbon surfactants per unit volume) and therefore are often used where other substances cannot deliver the required performance, or where PFAS can be used in a much smaller amount and with the same performance as a higher amount of a non-fluorinated chemical. Examples are uses that operate over wide temperature ranges or uses that require extremely stable and non-reactive substances. The C-F bonds in PFAS lead to very stable substances, a feature that also makes them very persistent in the environment.

span.label: PTFE
span.quote: We can ascertain from the SPIN database that two PFAS, 1H-pentafluoroethane and PTFE, account for 75% of the quantities used in the Nordic countries. One explanation is that PTFE and 1H-pentafluoroethanes are not used as additives, but as the main products. For example, entire roof structures or coatings are made of out of PTFE.

span.label: what counts as a PFAS - UNDER BUCK ET AL. 2011: aliphatic substances with the -CnF2n+1 moiety, n at least 1
span.quote: A first clear definition of PFAS was provided by Buck et al. (2011). They defined PFAS as aliphatic substances with the moiety -CnF2n+1 where n is at least 1. The OECD/UNEP Global PFC Group noted that many substances, containing other perfluorocarbon moieties (e.g. -CnF2n-), were not commonly recognized as PFAS according to Buck et al. (2011), e.g. perfluorodicarboxylic acids. Considering their structural similarities to commonly recognized PFAS with the -CnF2n+1 moiety, the OECD/UNEP Global PFC Group proposed to also include substances that contain the moiety -CnF2n- (n ≥ 1) as PFAS. The present study is in line with this proposal.

span.label: what counts as a PFAS - UNDER THE OECD/UNEP PROPOSAL: also substances containing -CnF2n-, on grounds of structural similarity
span.quote: A first clear definition of PFAS was provided by Buck et al. (2011). They defined PFAS as aliphatic substances with the moiety -CnF2n+1 where n is at least 1. The OECD/UNEP Global PFC Group noted that many substances, containing other perfluorocarbon moieties (e.g. -CnF2n-), were not commonly recognized as PFAS according to Buck et al. (2011), e.g. perfluorodicarboxylic acids. Considering their structural similarities to commonly recognized PFAS with the -CnF2n+1 moiety, the OECD/UNEP Global PFC Group proposed to also include substances that contain the moiety -CnF2n- (n ≥ 1) as PFAS. The present study is in line with this proposal.

span.label: what counts as a PFAS - IN THIS STUDY: the OECD position plus both-ended perfluorocarbon chains, side-chain aromatics and fluorinated cycloaliphatics, minus non-polymers carrying only -CF3 or -CF2- except the ethers. The 1400 is a count under this one
span.quote: In contrast to the definition by Buck et al. (2011), the present study also includes i) substances where a perfluorocarbon chain is connected with functional groups on both ends, ii) aromatic substances that have perfluoroalkyl moieties on the side chains, and iii) fluorinated cycloaliphatic substances. More specifically, the present study focuses on polymeric PFAS with the -CF2- moiety and non-polymeric PFAS with the -CF2-CF2- moiety. It does not include non-polymeric substances that only contain a -CF3 or -CF2- moiety, with the exception of perfluoroalkylethers and per- and polyfluoroalkylether-based substances.

span.label: the number of PFAS per use category - AS THE PAPER MEANS IT: what this search identified
span.quote: It should be noted that the number of PFAS reflects the number that we have identified in the present study, and not the number of substances on the market or available for a certain use. For half of the use categories, we have identified more than 20 PFAS, and for seven use categories more than 100 PFAS.

span.label: the number of PFAS per use category - AS IT WILL BE READ: the number on the market for that use, which the authors say explicitly it is not
span.quote: It should be noted that the number of PFAS reflects the number that we have identified in the present study, and not the number of substances on the market or available for a certain use. For half of the use categories, we have identified more than 20 PFAS, and for seven use categories more than 100 PFAS.

span.label: a link between a PFAS and a use - FROM A PATENT: 42% of the 2400 links, and a patent shows a substance may be used, not that it is
span.quote: Of the 2400 links between individual PFAS and assigned uses, around 42% of the links were obtained from patents, 27% from studies that detected PFAS in products and 31% from publications that reported actual uses.

span.label: a link between a PFAS and a use - FROM AN ANALYTICAL DETECTION: 27%, and a detected substance may be an impurity or a degradation product rather than an ingredient
span.quote: These studies are important because they show in which products PFAS exist. However, in most studies only a handful of substances were analysed and even for these substances it is not clear whether they were used intentionally, impurities in the actual substances or degradation products.

span.label: extends → Kissa (2001), the standard monograph on PFAS as surfactants and repellents, which listed 39 use categories mostly from patents and is nearly twenty years old - this study finds five times as many uses
span.quote: A good overview of the range of uses of PFAS as surfactants and repellents is provided in the monograph by Kissa (2001). It lists 39 use categories, mostly derived from patents, and describes the function of PFAS in these use categories. However, the work by Kissa (2001) was published nearly 20 years ago, focused on fluorosurfactants and repellents, and it is not clear which of these uses are still relevant today.

span.label: critiques → confidential business information as it operates under TSCA - it leaves even regulators without volumes, use categories or substance identities, which limits their ability to assess and prevent harm
span.quote: The TSCA reform in the US was unfortunately unsuccessful in reducing industry’s excessive use of CBI. Even though CBI may protect a specific industry’s business, it results in overall less protection for consumers, users, and workers from the chemicals. Even regulators are left in the dark about volumes, use categories, and PFAS used, which limits their ability to assess and prevent harm to humans and the environment.

span.label: critiques → the voluntary phase-outs of PFOS- and PFOA-related substances, which other companies were not prevented from succeeding to and which saw very limited enforcement
span.quote: However, other companies have not been prevented from taking over the market, and there has been very limited enforcement of the actual phase-out through regulation. A recent article revealed that PFAS that can break down into PFOA and PFOS are still in use in the US. Those uses include coatings for medical devices, apparel, and other industries, and equipment in pharmaceutical companies. PFAS that can break down into PFOA and PFOS are also still used in semiconductor and electronics companies.

span.label: qualifies → its own inventory - not exhaustive, bounded by every register's exclusions, with 4% of functions and 21% of enabling properties undetermined
span.quote: However, as can be seen from the question marks in the Appendix it was not always possible to determine why PFAS were used or needed in a particular case. In 4% of the cases we could not clarify which function the PFAS fulfil in the use category or subcategory, and in 21% of the cases we could not clarify which property is needed to fulfil the mentioned function. For example, we do not know exactly why PFAS are employed in the ventilation of respiratory airways, in brake-pad additives, and in resilient linoleum.

span.label: extends → the Montreal Protocol's essential-use concept, argued here in its default-deny form: treat every use as non-essential unless a case is made, with a sunset clause on those accepted
span.quote: The approach of allowing PFAS only in “essential uses”, as suggested for example in the EU strategy paper “Elements for an EU-strategy for PFAS”, will not be easy to implement if regulators try to assess all uses individually. An alternative approach could be to deem all PFAS uses as “non-essential” unless producers or users make a convincing case for essentiality, and that authorities set a sunset clause on “essential uses”.

span.label: articles —distinct-from→ SPIN database
span.note: differs in: whether the substance is in a preparation the register requires or in an article it does not · the relation itself is separately evidenced · strength of the relation: 0.95
span.quote: Also, the substances included in the present study from the SPIN database are not substances in articles, but substances in preparations.

span.label: CBI —distinct-from→ SPIN database
span.note: differs in: whether a quantity is in the register's public half or its confidential one · the relation itself is separately evidenced · strength of the relation: 0.95
span.quote: The data from the US are only partly helpful, because a large part of the reported amounts is CBI and only substances above 11.34 t at a single site have been reported. Although in some use categories large quantities of PFAS are employed, it is difficult to compare the amounts, because the unreported amounts due to CBI could be much larger than the non-confidential reported amounts. The extent of the uncertainties in the SPIN database due to the CBI cannot be estimated with the available data, but could be large.

span.label: patents —distinct-from→ use categories
span.note: differs in: whether the evidence is that a use was invented or that it happens · the relation itself is separately evidenced · strength of the relation: 0.95
span.quote: It lists 39 use categories, mostly derived from patents, and describes the function of PFAS in these use categories.

span.label: more than 200 uses in 64 categories were identified for more than 1400 individual PFAS - five times the uses in the standard previous compilation
span.term: more than 200 uses in 64 categories were identified for more than 1400 individual PFAS - five times the uses in the standard previous compilation
span.quote: In the present study, more than 200 uses in 64 use categories were identified for more than 1400 individual PFAS. This means that the present study encompasses five times as many uses (counted as use categories plus subcategories) than included by Kissa (2001). This shows that the present study goes much further than simply updating this previous work.

span.label: the count of substances is a count of what this search found and explicitly not the number on the market, and the authors say so before giving the numbers

span.quote: It should be noted that the number of PFAS reflects the number that we have identified in the present study, and not the number of substances on the market or available for a certain use. For half of the use categories, we have identified more than 20 PFAS, and for seven use categories more than 100 PFAS.

span.label: more than 80% of the US volume entries are confidential, and the size of the resulting uncertainty cannot be estimated from the available data

span.quote: Of the 2400 links between individual PFAS and assigned uses, around 42% of the links were obtained from patents, 27% from studies that detected PFAS in products and 31% from publications that reported actual uses.

span.label: two substances account for 75% of PFAS quantity in the Nordic registers, because they are the product rather than an additive
span.term: two substances account for 75% of PFAS quantity in the Nordic registers, because they are the product rather than an additive
span.quote: We can ascertain from the SPIN database that two PFAS, 1H-pentafluoroethane and PTFE, account for 75% of the quantities used in the Nordic countries. One explanation is that PTFE and 1H-pentafluoroethanes are not used as additives, but as the main products. For example, entire roof structures or coatings are made of out of PTFE.

span.label: substances that break down into PFOA and PFOS remain in use in medical device coatings, apparel, pharmaceutical equipment and semiconductor manufacture after the voluntary phase-outs
span.term: substances that break down into PFOA and PFOS remain in use in medical device coatings, apparel, pharmaceutical equipment and semiconductor manufacture after the voluntary phase-outs
span.quote: However, other companies have not been prevented from taking over the market, and there has been very limited enforcement of the actual phase-out through regulation. A recent article revealed that PFAS that can break down into PFOA and PFOS are still in use in the US. Those uses include coatings for medical devices, apparel, and other industries, and equipment in pharmaceutical companies. PFAS that can break down into PFOA and PFOS are also still used in semiconductor and electronics companies.

span.label: a single cell phone contains fluoropolymer wiring, PFAS in the circuit boards and a fluoropolymer screen coating - three applications in one product
span.term: a single cell phone contains fluoropolymer wiring, PFAS in the circuit boards and a fluoropolymer screen coating - three applications in one product
span.quote: Some consumer products even have multiple applications of PFAS within the same product. A cell phone for example contains fluoropolymer wiring, PFAS in the circuit boards/semiconductors, and a screen coated with a fingerprint-resistant fluoropolymer. The search for alternatives is therefore a very challenging and extensive task.

span.label: defined by Buck et al. (2011) as aliphatic substances with the -CnF2n+1 moiety; widened by the OECD/UNEP group to include -CnF2n-; and widened again here to both-ended chains, side-chain aromatics and cycloaliphatics
span.quote: A first clear definition of PFAS was provided by Buck et al. (2011). They defined PFAS as aliphatic substances with the moiety -CnF2n+1 where n is at least 1. The OECD/UNEP Global PFC Group noted that many substances, containing other perfluorocarbon moieties (e.g. -CnF2n-), were not commonly recognized as PFAS according to Buck et al. (2011), e.g. perfluorodicarboxylic acids. Considering their structural similarities to commonly recognized PFAS with the -CnF2n+1 moiety, the OECD/UNEP Global PFC Group proposed to also include substances that contain the moiety -CnF2n- (n ≥ 1) as PFAS. The present study is in line with this proposal.

span.label: confidential business information - the status of more than 80% of the volume entries in the US Chemical Data Reporting database
span.quote: Under the TSCA, the Chemical Data Reporting lists under “volume” the amount of a substance in a certain sector and function category or product category. However, more than 80% of the volume entries in the Chemical Data Reporting database are CBI. The certainty of the available information is therefore low, but a general statement is still possible.

span.label: individual PFAS with an identified use - a count under this study's definition, which is wider than Buck 2011 in three ways and narrower in one
span.quote: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are of concern because of their very high persistence and impacts on human and environmental health. Currently, many different PFAS (on the order of several thousands) are used in a wide range of applications and there is no comprehensive source of information on the many individual substances and their functions in different applications. Here we provide a broad overview of many use categories where PFAS have been employed and for which function; we also specify which PFAS have been used and discuss the magnitude of the uses. Our compilation is not exhaustive, but it was still possible to demonstrate that PFAS are used in almost all industry branches and many consumer products. In total, more than 200 use categories and subcategories were identified for more than 1400 individual PFAS.

span.label: metric tons at a single site - the TSCA reporting threshold, below which a substance does not appear at all
span.quote: Manufacturers and importers that produced chemicals in amounts exceeding 25’000 pounds (11.34 metric tons, t) at a site in the US between 2012 and 2015 were obliged to report to the US Environmental Protection Agency (US EPA) in 2016 (data for 2016 to 2019 will be reported in 2020). The data reported in 2016 (available in CSV files) included for each reported substance the name, Chemical Abstracts Service (CAS) registry number and product categories for consumer and commercial uses and sectors, as well as function categories for industrial processing and use. The masses (tonnages) used and exported also had to be reported; however, they are in most cases confidential business information (CBI).

Examples are “surface active agents in all other basic inorganic chemical manufacturing”, or “functional fluids in wholesale and retail trade”. The PFAS listed under such categories and their quantities were not, therefore, considered in the present study.
